model.label: Tax-funded universal public insurance (Medicare) with free public hospitals, alongside subsidised voluntary private insurance

overview.statement: Medicare, the public insurance scheme, covers Australian and New Zealand citizens, permanent residents and people from countries with reciprocal agreements; some migrants, refugees and humanitarian entrants qualify depending on their visa, and other residents must buy private cover.
Universal public coverage first arrived with Medibank in 1975, was wound back and dismantled by 1981, and was restored in 1984 as Medicare, paid for by a 1% income levy plus general taxation.

The federal government sets health policy, funds Medicare and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS), regulates medicines, devices and private insurance, and helps fund public hospitals, which state and territory governments run.

Medicare pays doctors fee-for-service through the Medicare Benefits Schedule (MBS); public hospitals are paid partly by activity, priced against a national cost standard, and partly through block budgets for services that cannot be paid per activity.

Public hospitals, owned and run by state governments, treat patients without charge; services outside public hospitals are run by private for-profit or not-for-profit providers, and Medicare subsidises part of what patients pay for them.

locator.section: Universal health care and private health insurance in Australia

financing.statement: Most taxpayers pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income; people with lower incomes pay less or nothing.
Governments paid for 74% of total health expenditure in 2023-24.
Hospital care cost AUD 114 billion in 2023-24, 42% of all health spending; state and territory governments funded 47% of it, the federal government 36% and non-government sources 17%.

High-income earners without private hospital cover pay a Medicare levy surcharge, now up to 1.5% of taxable income; in 2024-25 it applied from AUD 97,000 for individuals and AUD 194,000 for families, and people earning less can receive a government contribution towards private premiums.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

financing.statement: Individuals pay about 15% of all health spending directly as out-of-pocket fees, close to twice the share contributed by private health insurers.
Recurrent spending on public hospitals was AUD 103.1 billion in 2023-24 (excluding depreciation); 94% came from the federal, state and territory governments and 6% from non-government sources.

covered.statement: Medicare pays 100% of the schedule fee for GP visits, 85% for most specialist services outside hospital and 75% for treatment in private hospitals; patients pay any remaining gap.
Public hospital care is covered in full, and most medicines are subsidised through the PBS for everyone covered by Medicare.

Medicare covers preventive, inpatient, outpatient, maternity, primary, mental health, palliative and rehabilitative care and home visits, with mental health patients able to claim 10 sessions a year with a professional.

Dental care, glasses and contact lenses, assistive devices and ambulance services are generally outside Medicare (eye tests are covered); dental care and emergency transport are mostly paid privately, though some states, territories or councils fund ambulances.

A medicine reaches the PBS only after Therapeutic Goods Administration approval and review by the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee; if it adds health benefit at reasonable cost compared with existing treatment, the federal government negotiates its listing with the supplier.
Health technology assessment is used with the aim that Medicare pays only for treatments that are clinically effective, cost-effective and safe.

Allied health care is mostly outside Medicare, which subsidises some services for people with complex needs or chronic conditions; in 2022-23, 39% of Australians used at least one Medicare-subsidised allied health service.

cost_sharing.statement: Patients pay nothing when a doctor bulk bills, that is, bills Medicare directly. The national share of doctors who bulk bill has declined gradually in recent years, and as of October 2024 annual bulk-billing rates ran from 53.2% in the Australian Capital Territory to 82.2% in New South Wales.

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

cost_sharing.statement: In 2022, 82% of GP services were bulk billed; where patients were charged, they paid $43 per visit on average, with regional averages between $16 and $99.
Providers may charge more than the MBS schedule fee, and in that case patients usually pay the difference themselves.

Under the Original Medicare Safety Net, once a person's gap payments in a year pass a threshold (AUD 576 in 2025), Medicare pays 100% instead of 85% of the schedule fee for further out-of-hospital MBS services.

Under the Extended Medicare Safety Net, once out-of-pocket costs pass a yearly threshold (AUD 2,616 in 2025), Medicare covers 80% of further out-of-pocket costs for eligible out-of-hospital MBS care; concession cardholders and some families reach a lower threshold.

For certain specialist services, the Greatest Permissible Gap caps the difference between the MBS fee and the Medicare benefit, so Medicare pays more than 85% when fees are high; the cap was AUD 105 as at 1 November 2025.
The standard PBS co-payment was cut from AUD 43 to AUD 30 in 2023; further measures froze it at AUD 32 until 2026, and at AUD 8 for concession cardholders until 2030.
The average cost of a specialist visit rose from AUD 140 to AUD 153, faster than Medicare rebates, and Medicare's share of specialist visit costs fell from 64% in 2012-13 to 55% in 2022-23.

In 2020-21, only 44% of private hospital admissions carried no out-of-pocket fee and only 34% of specialist attendances were bulk billed; non-bulk-billed visits cost patients $98 on average for specialists outside hospital and $303 for obstetric care.

locator.section: Universal health care and private health insurance in Australia

cost_sharing.statement: Private providers set their own fees to cover costs and earn profits, and the Constitution excludes the government from regulating the fees they charge.

locator.section: User fees and the role of the market in setting price

cost_sharing.statement: In 2024-25, 77.9% of non-referred GP services and 28.2% of specialist services were bulk billed, so the patient paid nothing at the point of care.

cost_sharing.statement: In 2024-25, 49.1% of patients had all their services bulk billed, a turn upward after falling from a peak of 67.6% in 2020-21.

locator.section: Indicator results: bulk billing and out-of-pocket costs

cost_sharing.statement: Among Medicare services in 2024-25, out-of-pocket costs were highest for specialists (AUD 126), followed by allied health services (AUD 71) and non-referred GP services (AUD 49).

locator.section: Indicator results: bulk billing and out-of-pocket costs

cost_sharing.statement: In 2024-25, 7.7% of people who needed a GP delayed or skipped the visit because of cost, down from 8.8% in 2023-24, after rising every year from 2.4% in 2020-21.

locator.section: Indicator results: 3. Selected potentially preventable hospitalisations / affordability, Measure 1

financial_hardship.statement: A systematic review of 19 Australian studies (over 70,000 people affected by cancer) found that financial burden after a cancer diagnosis is common; younger patients, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, rural and remote residents, low-income and unemployed people, and privately insured patients faced higher risk.

In one survey of 289 men with prostate cancer included in that review, the median out-of-pocket cost of treatment was AUD 8,000; to pay, 38% drew on savings, 8% sold assets and 22% raised their credit card limits.

A 2025 review of 37 qualitative studies found that people with chronic conditions lost income through reduced work, struggled with up-front fees, co-payments and medicine costs, found cost the largest barrier to dental care, and traded off health care against basic living needs, especially those who earned too much for welfare support.

additional_care.statement: Private insurance pays for treatment as a private patient in public or private hospitals and for services Medicare excludes, such as dental and ambulance; it is sold as hospital, extras and ambulance cover, and insurers may not cover Medicare-funded out-of-hospital services such as GP visits and diagnostic tests.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: Everyone has public coverage, and about 55% of the population also holds private insurance.
Among OECD countries, duplicate private insurance, which buys faster access or wider choice of provider alongside public cover, was most widespread in Australia and Ireland.

Voluntary private hospital insurance uses community-rated premiums, which make young, healthy members predictably profitable and elderly or chronically ill members predictably loss-making for insurers; a risk equalisation scheme is used to counter this.

In a privately insured cohort in one New South Wales health district (2010-2015), 40% of people with a hospital stay used only public hospitals, and only 62% of overnight admissions were claimed on private insurance.

Being liable for the Medicare levy surcharge in a given year raised the probability of buying private hospital insurance by 2 to 3 percent that year, and by 13 percent after a decade of continued liability.
Larger private insurance rebates for people over 65 produced only a modest rise in take-up, with price elasticities of -0.1 to -0.2 in the first two years; low-income older people responded more.

access.statement: Patients usually need a referral from a primary care provider to see a specialist; without one, they receive a lower Medicare rebate or pay the whole fee.
In 2024-25, half of public hospital elective surgery patients were admitted within 45 days of joining the waiting list (46 days in 2023-24), and 90% within 329 days, the same as the year before.

locator.section: Indicator results: 4. Waiting times for admitted patient services, Measure 1

access.statement: In 2024-25, half of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients on elective surgery waiting lists were admitted within 59 days, a longer wait than the 45 days for other Australians.

locator.section: Indicator results: 1. Equity of access by selected equity groups, Measure 3

access.statement: In 2024-25, 53.4% of emergency department patients left the department (admitted, transferred or discharged) within four hours, the lowest share since a peak of 73.2% in 2015-16.

locator.section: Indicator results: 2. Emergency department waiting times, Measure 2

access.statement: In 2024-25, 18.3% of people aged 15 and over delayed or did not see a medical specialist when they needed to, down from 20.5% in 2023-24; for GPs the shares were 26.6% and 29.2%.

locator.section: Barriers to health service use: delayed or did not use health services when needed

access.statement: Staff shortages are worst in remote areas, which in 2022 had 53 full-time-equivalent specialists per 100,000 people against 160 in major cities.
In 2023, 86% of psychiatrists worked in major cities and fewer than 1%, 19 psychiatrists in all, in remote and very remote areas.
By 2023, 82% of health professions reported workforce shortages, and the share of job vacancies filled fell from 60% in 2022 to 44% in 2023, largely because of skill gaps.
Australia relies increasingly on doctors trained abroad: 32% of medical practitioners in 2022, up from 29% in 2013, including 51% of intensive care specialists and about 44% of GPs.

Among people with at least four GP visits in two years (about 80% of the population), roughly one in three had high continuity with a single GP across 2016-17 to 2022-23; high continuity was more common among people with greater care needs but much less common in very remote areas.

In 2024-25, cost was a reason for delaying or skipping care when needed for 16.1% of people aged 15 and over in the case of dental professionals, 8.6% for medical specialists, 7.7% for GPs and 2.1% for hospitals, all lower than in 2023-24.

locator.section: Delayed or did not use health services when needed - due to cost

access.statement: Cost-related delays in dental care were strongly linked to disadvantage in 2024-25: 23.1% of people in the most disadvantaged areas delayed or skipped a dental professional because of cost, against 9.6% in the least disadvantaged areas.

locator.section: Delayed or did not use health services when needed - due to cost

access.statement: In 2024-25, 26.0% of people who saw a GP said they waited longer than they found acceptable for an appointment, down from 28.0% in 2023-24 but up from 18.9% in 2015-16.
Of the people who saw a GP for urgent care in 2024-25, 41.6% were seen within four hours, against 63.6% in 2015-16, and 47.0% waited 24 hours or longer.

locator.section: Indicator results: GP waiting times for urgent medical care

outcomes.statement: There were 99.1 potentially avoidable deaths per 100,000 people in 2024, slightly more than the 98.6 recorded for 2023.

The age-standardised death rate in very remote areas was 1.6 times that of major cities over 2018-2022; First Nations people, 32% of the remote and very remote population, lived on average eight years less than non-Indigenous people in 2020-2022, and 12 years less in remote and very remote areas.
In 2023 Australia was among the five countries with the lowest 30-day in-hospital death rates after admission for heart attack (under 4%, patients aged 45 and over, unlinked data).

locator.section: Chapter 6: Mortality following acute myocardial infarction

outcomes.statement: The OECD cites Australia, with Norway and Belgium, as having below-average cancer mortality despite relatively high cancer incidence, which it attributes in part to earlier diagnosis and treatment.
In 2016 Australia was in the top decile of the Healthcare Access and Quality Index, one of a few countries outside Europe there alongside Canada, Japan and New Zealand.
For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the potentially avoidable death rate over 2020-24 was 309.0 per 100,000, the highest in the reported series, which starts with 2017-21.
In the GBD 2019 study, Australia's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 90.2 (95% uncertainty interval 88.1-91.7) in 2019, 14.4 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 study, Australia's HAQ Index score rose from 83.9 in 1990 to 90.4 in 2000 and 95.9 in 2016.

locator.table: Table 2: HAQ Index (95% UI), columns 1990, 2000 and 2016

costs.statement: Health spending reached 10.1% of GDP in 2023-24, compared with an average of 8.1% across high-income countries.
COVID-19 drove a sharp rise in spending, from AUD 203 billion in 2019-20 to AUD 241 billion in 2021-22, before spending eased slightly in real terms in 2022-23 back towards its pre-pandemic trend.
Australia, like Israel, has relatively high health care prices compared with the OECD average, though below Iceland, Switzerland and the United States.
Australia was among a group of countries, with Canada and several Western European countries, spending between USD 7,000 and USD 8,500 per person on health, below Switzerland, Norway and Germany.
In 2016 Australia spent 9.6% of GDP on health, the lowest among the high-income countries compared, against 17.8% in the United States and 12.4% in Switzerland.
Government spending per person on PBS medicines rose 13% between 2021-22 and 2022-23, driven by inflation, lower co-payments and new high-cost medicines.
Out-of-pocket payments fell from 20.6% of total health spending in 2000 to 15.3% in 2022, still slightly above the high-income-country average of 13.2%.

what_works.statement: Price discounts the government negotiates for PBS medicines meant that, while pharmaceutical spending grew 23% from 2010 to 2018, net pharmaceutical revenue grew only 5% from 2010 to 2019.
Avoidable mortality was 97 deaths per 100,000 people in 2023, against 158 across OECD countries.

Bulk billing of GP services was more common in poorer areas in 2022: 86% in the most disadvantaged areas against 73% in the least disadvantaged, and rates in remote areas did not differ significantly from metropolitan ones.

Higher incentives, introduced in 2022, for GPs to bulk bill children and concession card holders in rural and remote areas raised GP visits by 2.7% and bulk-billed visits by 9.0%, and cut the out-of-pocket cost per visit by 13.0%, for rural residents relative to urban residents.

A 2025 review concluded that Australian health policies effectively lower the financial burden of care for many people, while groups who do not qualify for concessional thresholds still face distinct difficulties.

problems.statement: Between 2006 and 2014, people in the lowest income decile had 15 times the odds of catastrophic health spending (10% or more of household income, counting practitioner fees, medicines and insurance premiums) as those in the highest decile, after adjustment; the share with catastrophic spending rose from 13% to 19% in decile 2 and from 7% to 13% in decile 3.

Using 2014-15 Medicare data, specialist visits favoured people in wealthier areas; visits with out-of-pocket costs were distributed in favour of the rich, and the slightly pro-poor spread of free (bulk-billed) visits did not offset this.
For GP visits that were not bulk billed in 2022, patients in remote areas paid more on average ($56) than those in metropolitan areas ($43).
A 2026 simulation study found that the current risk equalisation scheme for private hospital insurance leaves strong incentives for insurers to select risks and weak incentives to control spending.

The gains from this rural bulk-billing incentive reform were uneven: effects were larger for people with higher initial out-of-pocket costs, such as adults, people without concession cards and residents of less disadvantaged areas, and inequities in access persisted.
In 2024, 77% of adults aged 75 and over in Australia took five or more medications, the highest rate among reporting OECD countries, although Australia recorded one of the largest declines over time.
Australia had 6.4 mental hospital beds per 100,000 people in 2020, against 28.6 in other high-income countries.
Medicare rules let after-hours deputising services bill higher out-of-hours rates that GPs working from their own clinics cannot, which discourages practices from opening late.
The 31 Primary Health Networks that commission local services vary widely in performance; in 2025 over half of GPs rated their local network's value as poor or very poor.

Recognition of overseas medical qualifications is considerably harder in Australia than in the UK, New Zealand and Canada; overseas practitioners cite lack of recognition of their experience and complex, costly accreditation.
In 2021-22, 69% of residential aged care providers reported operating losses.

reforms.statement: The Aged Care Act 2024, in force since November 2025, set new person-centred care standards meant to help older people make informed decisions about their care and stay independent.
A National Lung Cancer Screening Program was launched in July 2025, designed in line with recommendations of the Medical Services Advisory Committee.
With the number of older people using home care projected to grow by about 44,000 a year to nearly 2 million by 2042, the government introduced the Support at Home Program in 2025.

To speed up hiring of foreign-trained staff, in October 2024 the government launched an Expedited Specialist Pathway that lets eligible specialists credentialed in Ireland, New Zealand and the UK fast-track their specialist registration.
In 2024 the federal government introduced payments of up to AUD 21,000 a year for GPs to attract doctors to rural and remote areas.

MyMedicare, a voluntary patient registration scheme introduced in October 2023 to strengthen continuity of care, had broad support in principle, but practice staff interviewed in 2025-2026 reported limited benefits so far and a heavy administrative burden that could undermine continuity.

From 1 November 2025, Medicare bulk billing incentive payments, previously limited to children under 16 and concession card holders, became claimable whenever any Medicare-eligible patient is bulk billed, under amended MBS regulations.

locator.section: Summary of MBS Changes for 1 November 2025: Bulk Billing Changes

reforms.statement: Since 2023, patients whose conditions are stable and ongoing may obtain a two-month (60-day) supply of their mental health medicines for one prescription co-payment (AUD 32 as of January 2024); more than 300 PBS-listed medicines fall under the policy.

In February 2025 the government committed AUD 7.9 billion to extend the tripled GP bulk billing incentives to all Medicare-eligible patients and to create a Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program, under which practices that bulk bill every patient for every consultation receive a quarterly payment of 12.5% of their MBS revenue.

locator.section: Why are the changes being made?

reforms.statement: In November 2023 the government tripled the bulk-billing incentive payments for consultations with concession card holders and children.

us_lessons.statement: Comparing the US with other high-income countries, researchers found the US spent roughly twice as much while using care at similar rates; prices of labour and goods, including medicines, and administrative costs were the main drivers of the gap.
In the same comparison, administrative costs made up 8% of US health spending against 1% to 3% in the other countries.

Between 2013 and 2017, government-paid prices for three costly drugs (adalimumab, ranibizumab and aflibercept) fell faster each year in Australia than in the United States; aflibercept's price fell 16.9% a year in Australia against 1.5% in the US.
The authors of the US-Australia drug price comparison caution that their data do not explain why prices diverged or what actions would change future prices in either country.
